entry.title: Climatic extremes and their social implications in 17<sup>th</sup> century Transylvania: An historical climate reconstruction

link.title: Climatic extremes and their social implications in 17<sup>th</sup> century Transylvania: An historical climate reconstruction
(PDF) Climatic extremes and their social implications in 17<sup>th</sup> century Transylvania: An historical climate reconstruction
(XML) Climatic extremes and their social implications in 17<sup>th</sup> century Transylvania: An historical climate reconstruction

entry.content:
by Ovidiu Razvan Gaceu, Tudor Caciora, Mihai Dudaș, Ștefan Baias, Marius Stupariu, Maria Maxim, Cătălina Mărculeț

The 17th century was a period of significant climatic and social challenges in Europe, marked by the transition to the Maunder Minimum, as part of the Little Ice Age; marked by low solar activity, many negative thermal anomalies, long and harsh winters, rainy years, numerous extreme weather phenomena, famines, epidemics, etc. Taking these aspects into account, the present study aims to reconstruct, based on written historical sources, the climatic variability in the Principality of Transylvania during the 17th century. The emphasis is placed on reconstructing anomalies in temperature and precipitation regimes, as well as on analysing climate-related calamities and their impacts on society. The analysis identified a high prevalence of events associated with abnormally cold weather, with 55 winters mentioned as particularly harsh in this century; 36 of these occurred during the Maunder Minimum (between 1645 and 1700, which falls within our study period). This interval was also characterised by numerous episodes of excessive precipitation, especially during winter, and a clear imbalance between events associated with excessive humidity and those associated with drought. Variable climatic conditions caused poor harvests, famine, high prices and favoured the emergence of severe epidemics (especially plague) and social crises. The correlation of historical sources with other proxy data from natural archives confirms the exceptional character of this century and validates the reconstruction based on historical sources. They also indicate that natural factors, such as solar activity and general atmospheric circulation, could have generated the colder and wetter climatic conditions in 17th century Transylvania, particularly during the winters of the Maunder Minimum.

entry.title: Engaged research and its implications for transformation in climate adaptation sciences

link.title: Engaged research and its implications for transformation in climate adaptation sciences
(PDF) Engaged research and its implications for transformation in climate adaptation sciences
(XML) Engaged research and its implications for transformation in climate adaptation sciences

entry.content:
by Katherine Cann

Transformative climate adaptation efforts, which call for the fundamental reshaping of social systems that inform vulnerability to climate risk, introduce significant ethical and procedural questions for researchers. Engaged research practices, such as co-production and participatory action research, may be useful in addressing these complex questions and pushing adaptation research towards more transformative ends. However, there are also ethical and procedural concerns plaguing participatory knowledge production, and scholars claim engaged research efforts have failed to meet goals for transforming scientific practice. Recent literature in adaptation, climate services, sustainability science, and environmental governance, illustrates the ongoing challenges and unresolved tensions holding engaged research practices back from its transformative aims. This essay suggests three areas of growth for engaged researchers in climate services and adaptation: interrogate the aims of research projects, focus on learning outcomes, and evaluate research governance. The essay addresses a wide audience and serves three primary purposes: 1) as a primer for students and early career researchers beginning to explore the history and use of engaged research in climate services and adaptation, 2) as a summary of common challenges for researchers designing and implementing engaged research projects with communities and other stakeholders, and 3) as a blueprint for institutional supporters, including funders and research convenors aiming to improve engaged research outcomes and advance more transformative adaptation.

entry.title: Climate change impacts on the predicted performance of optimized building-integrated photovoltaics

link.title: Climate change impacts on the predicted performance of optimized building-integrated photovoltaics
(PDF) Climate change impacts on the predicted performance of optimized building-integrated photovoltaics
(XML) Climate change impacts on the predicted performance of optimized building-integrated photovoltaics

entry.content:
by Elyas Hannoufa, Eric Johlin

Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) are a promising strategy for enhancing building energy performance and reducing carbon emissions. However, most design optimization studies rely on historical climate datasets that may fail to capture the operating conditions buildings will experience under climate change. This study develops a computational framework for the multi-objective optimization of BIPV envelope systems using future climate projections from the CanESM5 model under the SSP3-7.0 scenario. We analyze two system configurations, awning shades and thin-film window coatings, across four cities with diverse climates (Berlin, Los Angeles, Chicago, Singapore), comparing results from conventional EPW files, NASA 2023 historical data, and 2046–2050 climate scenarios. Optimization integrates electricity generation, thermal loads, and daylighting quality to capture building-level trade-offs. Results show that traditional EPW datasets systematically under-predict BIPV performance, particularly in Berlin and Los Angeles. Under 2046–2050 projected conditions, all four cities exhibit performance gains: substantial in Berlin, Chicago and Los Angeles, and marginal in Singapore, with the largest absolute gains in Los Angeles. By 2050, unshaded windows transition to consistently detrimental for building energy balance. Thin-film coatings achieve optimal outcomes at high absorptance, in the 80–90% range, contrary to current low-absorption design practice. Within the CanESM5 SSP3-7.0 scenario examined, these findings show that projected climate conditions can substantially reshape the modeled performance landscape of BIPV systems, emphasizing the need for forward-looking climate projections in building design optimization and the growing importance of BIPV for climate-adaptive and resilient urban buildings.

entry.title: Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)

link.title: Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)
(PDF) Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)
(XML) Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)

entry.content:
by Alonso Ramírez, Marcelo Ardón, Pavel García, Nicholas S. Marzolf, David Genereux

Climate change is altering ecosystems worldwide, but long-term, site-level hydroclimatic responses remain comparatively under-documented in many tropical regions. We analyzed long-term air and water temperature, precipitation, and stream water level data from two active Caribbean research sites: La Selva Research Station, Costa Rica, and El Verde Field Station, Puerto Rico. Our goal was to assess long-term hydroclimatic trends and changes in extreme events using continuous monitoring from automatic and manual sensors. Long-term records show a mean daily temperature of 25.1°C (1992–2024, range: 19.5-29.6°C) at La Selva and 23.6°C (2000–2024, range: 17.7-28.2°C) at El Verde. Mean annual precipitation is 4166 mm at La Selva (1983–2024) and 3635.8 mm at El Verde (1975–2024). We found a decadal warming trend of 0.29°C at both locations. The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influenced air temperature at El Verde, where La Niña (+0.02°C day−1, 95% CI: 0.002–0.042) phase was associated with higher daily temperatures, but had no detectable effect on air temperature at La Selva. A significant increase in the frequency of extreme temperature events (defined as exceeding the 95th, 97th, and 99th percentiles) was observed at both sites. Using the 95th percentile and a fitted generalized linear model, both locations had ~8 extreme temperature events per year in the beginning and increased to ~35 events per year in 2024. Changes in precipitation extremes were site-specific and differed between wet and dry metrics. La Selva showed an increase in wet extremes (heavy precipitation), with 99th percentile rainfall exceedances rising from ~1 event per year (1983–1985) to 6 per year in 2024. In contrast, El Verde showed no significant increase in heavy-precipitation events, but exhibited an increase in dry extremes (dry days <1.4 mm, increasing from 152 to 170 days per year). Stream water temperature had a moderate but significant increase. At La Selva, water temperature increased by 0.2°C, and at El Verde, by 0.9°C. An increasing tendency in high-water-level conditions was observed at both locations, though with marginal statistical support (p = 0.08 for the 99th percentile at La Selva and 95th percentile at El Verde), with estimated durations above these extreme thresholds roughly doubling over the study period. Overall, our study shows an increasing frequency of extreme events, both wet and dry, at these two Caribbean protected locations. These findings suggest important and distinct regional changes in climate over the region, with important consequences for ecosystem conservation and management.

entry.title: How much climate-smart agriculture is enough? A dose-response analysis of technology adoption effects on farmer welfare in Ghana

link.title: How much climate-smart agriculture is enough? A dose-response analysis of technology adoption effects on farmer welfare in Ghana
(PDF) How much climate-smart agriculture is enough? A dose-response analysis of technology adoption effects on farmer welfare in Ghana
(XML) How much climate-smart agriculture is enough? A dose-response analysis of technology adoption effects on farmer welfare in Ghana

entry.content:
by Stephen Prah, John N. Ng’ombe, Bright Owusu Asante, Jonathan Masasi

Climate-smart agricultural technologies (CSAT) are promoted to enhance agricultural productivity and strengthen resilience to climate change. However, limited empirical evidence exists on the effects of adoption intensity, particularly when farmers adopt multiple technologies simultaneously. This study examines the effects of CSAT adoption intensity on maize yield and household asset accumulation in Ghana using survey data from 2,151 maize farmers. A dose–response model with Heckman selection is applied to address potential selection bias and estimate the causal effects of varying adoption levels. The findings show that farmers’ education, access to credit, extension services, and perceived drought significantly influence both the likelihood and intensity of CSAT adoption. Results reveal a U-shaped relationship between CSAT adoption intensity and maize yield, where yields initially decline but increase as adoption intensity rises. On average, higher CSAT adoption is associated with a 21% increase in maize yield. Similarly, CSAT intensity shows a nonlinear positive relationship with household asset accumulation, with an average 19.5% increase in assets. The results also indicate heterogeneous effects across farmers. Overall, higher CSAT adoption improves agricultural productivity and long-term household welfare, highlighting the need to strengthen extension services, expand credit access, and raise climate risk awareness to promote sustainable agricultural development.

entry.title: Comparison of data-driven and numerical weather prediction models for rainfall nowcasting in major cities of Bangladesh

link.title: Comparison of data-driven and numerical weather prediction models for rainfall nowcasting in major cities of Bangladesh
(PDF) Comparison of data-driven and numerical weather prediction models for rainfall nowcasting in major cities of Bangladesh
(XML) Comparison of data-driven and numerical weather prediction models for rainfall nowcasting in major cities of Bangladesh

entry.content:
by Sumia Akter, Jayeef Rahman Muaz, Rabiul Awal

Flood-prone Bangladesh requires accurate short-term rainfall prediction, yet conventional numerical weather prediction (NWP) models remain computationally intensive and regionally limited in skill. This study evaluates and compares four deep learning (DL) architectures — Simple Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Stacked LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) — against the physics-based Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model for one-hour-ahead rainfall forecasting across six climatologically diverse stations in Bangladesh. Each model was trained independently per station using hourly ERA5 reanalysis data spanning 2018–2024, and performance was assessed using both regression and binary detection metrics. Across the full test period, Simple LSTM achieved the strongest overall performance, explaining approximately 88% of ERA5 rainfall variance with the lowest prediction errors, while GRU produced nearly comparable results. Performance was consistently stronger at wetter stations such as Chittagong and Sylhet than at drier northwestern stations such as Rajshahi and Rangpur, where class imbalance and rainfall intermittency limited model skill. Event-category analysis across 10 WRF simulation events — spanning extreme, moderate, and weak rainfall regimes — showed that DL models demonstrated closest agreement with ERA5 reference values during extreme events, while skill declined notably during weak events due to near-zero rainfall conditions. WRF exhibited systematic overestimation, temporal displacement of peak rainfall, and strongly negative R² values across all event categories and stations. A Friedman test confirmed statistically significant differences in RMSE ranks among the four DL architectures (χ² = 10.60, p = 0.014), with a Nemenyi post-hoc test showing Simple LSTM significantly outperformed Stacked LSTM (p = 0.0095).

entry.title: From concept to action: Driving impact through responsible research practices in the International Polar Year 2032–2033 An early career perspective

link.title: From concept to action: Driving impact through responsible research practices in the International Polar Year 2032–2033 An early career perspective
(PDF) From concept to action: Driving impact through responsible research practices in the International Polar Year 2032–2033 An early career perspective
(XML) From concept to action: Driving impact through responsible research practices in the International Polar Year 2032–2033 An early career perspective

entry.content:
by Samuel G. Hartharn-Evans, Chloe Nunn, Amy Macfarlane, Natalia Banega, Anna Belcher, Radiance Calmer, Svenja Holste, Louise Mercer, Ningning Sun, M. A. J. van Soest, Zoe Wright

Regions at the poles are warming at rates two to four times higher than the global average, driving profound environmental, societal, and geopolitical changes. As Polar Early Career Researchers with careers extending into and beyond the 5th International Polar Year in 2032–2033, we have a responsibility to shape research practices that are impactful, ethical, and sustainable. We argue that current definitions of research impact often prioritize narrow, quantifiable metrics, overlooking cultural, environmental, and long-term consequences. Building on interdisciplinary workshops held in 2025 at the Polar Early Career World Summit (USA) and the Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UK), this paper redefines research impact for polar science and presents tangible action for integrating responsible practices ahead of the next IPY. We outline priorities across three levels: 1) individual researchers, who should practice reflexivity, promote interdisciplinarity, and implement environmentally responsible methods; 2) regional and national institutions, which must provide equitable funding, training, and inclusive protocols; 3) international IPY planning bodies, which should strengthen communication, publish guidelines, and implement regulations to prevent exploitative practices. Our call to action emphasizes collaboration, transparency, and improved impact evaluation frameworks to ensure that polar research delivers societal and environmental benefits while minimizing unintended consequences. This vision begins now and extends beyond the IPY, offering a roadmap for responsible polar science.

entry.title: Financing resilience, governing vulnerability: Adaptation finance as a form of political infrastructure

link.title: Financing resilience, governing vulnerability: Adaptation finance as a form of political infrastructure
(PDF) Financing resilience, governing vulnerability: Adaptation finance as a form of political infrastructure
(XML) Financing resilience, governing vulnerability: Adaptation finance as a form of political infrastructure

entry.content:
by Laurence L. Delina

Climate adaptation finance is commonly framed as a problem of insufficiency: too little money, too slowly deployed, and directed towards too many needs. This Essay argues that such framings obscure a more consequential question: who governs adaptation through finance. Rather than treating finance as a neutral flow of capital, it conceptualises adaptation finance as a form of political infrastructure, defined as the institutional arrangements, intermediaries, metrics, and decision rules that structure authority, prioritise certain vulnerabilities, and shape whose futures are rendered investable. Drawing on practices such as the Green Climate Fund’s readiness processes, creditworthiness-based urban resilience programs, and standardised risk metrics in sovereign and project appraisal, the Essay shows how adaptation priorities are increasingly mediated through financial criteria. These shifts are quietly reconfiguring power across scales. Financial rationalities originating in the Global North increasingly define what counts as credible adaptation in the Global South, often privileging risk reduction for capital over resilience for vulnerable communities. Shifting attention from funding gaps to governance infrastructures advances a distinct analytical intervention: adaptation finance is not simply underprovided, but structured by particular institutional logics. Recognising finance as governance reveals adaptation as a contested site of political authority, accountability, and justice, with implications for the legitimacy and equity of climate action.

entry.title: Global warming and the National Cattlemen’s Association 1986–1996

link.title: Global warming and the National Cattlemen’s Association 1986–1996
(PDF) Global warming and the National Cattlemen’s Association 1986–1996
(XML) Global warming and the National Cattlemen’s Association 1986–1996

entry.content:
by Jennifer Jacquet, Loredana Loy

In the mid-1980s, scientific studies first highlighted the role of anthropogenic methane in global warming and emissions from cows as an important source. This knowledge expanded views of responsibility for global warming beyond the fossil fuel sector. Using scientific studies, archival documents, media interviews, and various government reports, we analyzed how the National Cattlemen’s Association (NCA), a trade association for the U.S beef industry, reacted to news about its products’ impacts on global warming between 1986 and 1996. While previous studies have emphasized the role of trade associations in political lobbying, here we show that NCA responded mainly with strategic communications, including information gathering on civil society activities, commissioning academic experts to produce and share statistics that reframed scientific findings, and discursive tactics to influence politicians and the public. Despite scientific recommendations about opportunities to reduce methane emissions, we found no evidence that NCA researched or promoted any of these suggested changes to beef production. Instead, NCA treated global warming as a public relations concern that could affect consumer demand, rather than as a potentially serious consequence of beef production.

entry.title: No critical slowing down in the Atlantic Overturning Circulation in historical CMIP6 simulations

link.title: No critical slowing down in the Atlantic Overturning Circulation in historical CMIP6 simulations
(PDF) No critical slowing down in the Atlantic Overturning Circulation in historical CMIP6 simulations
(XML) No critical slowing down in the Atlantic Overturning Circulation in historical CMIP6 simulations

entry.content:
by Maya Ben-Yami, Lana Blaschke, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a key component of the Earth’s climate system, and has been suggested to have multiple stable states. Critical slowing down (CSD) can detect stability changes in Earth system components, and has been found in sea-surface temperature (SST) based fingerprints of the AMOC. Here, we look for CSD in historical simulations from 27 models from the sixth Climate Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6). We calculate three different CSD indicators for the AMOC streamfunction strengths at 26.5°N and 35°N, as well as for a previously suggested SST-based AMOC index (ASSTI) based on averaging SSTs in the subpolar gyre region. No model shows CSD in the ASSTI, which is in marked disagreement with observations. This lack of CSD is reflected in the AMOC streamfunctions in most models, although individual ensemble members in some models do show signs of CSD even under a conservative significance calculation. We thus conclude that: 1) The historical AMOC in CMIP6 models is not losing stability, 2) studies of AMOC stability should consider an ensemble of realisations, 3) there is no non-AMOC-related physical process in CMIP6 models which could cause signs of CSD in North-Atlantic SSTs in the 1850–2014 period, and thus the CSD in the observed ASSTI is likely a sign of a change in the AMOC. This final result suggests that observed changes in the ASSTI could indicate a loss of stability in the real-world AMOC.

entry.title: Inequities in heat-related emergency department visits in California from 2005 – 2017

link.title: Inequities in heat-related emergency department visits in California from 2005 – 2017
(PDF) Inequities in heat-related emergency department visits in California from 2005 – 2017
(XML) Inequities in heat-related emergency department visits in California from 2005 – 2017

entry.content:
by Marisa Donnelly, Brooke Lappe, Meredith Milet, Jason Vargo

Rising temperatures and extreme heat pose a substantial threat to human health through increases in heat-related morbidity and mortality. Moreover, social determinants of health can exacerbate the impact of heat on susceptible populations. This study investigates the inequities in heat-related emergency department (ED) visits in California from 2005-2017, focusing on how social determinants of health, represented by the California Healthy Places Index (HPI), may influence the associations between temperature and ED visits. A Distributed Lag Nonlinear Model (DLNM) was employed to assess the association between daily temperatures and ED visits for heat-related physical illness, mental health, and all-cause visits. The California HPI was used to stratify the data and evaluate disparities in heat-related ED visits across different socioeconomic conditions. There were 129,935,301 ED visits in California from 2005-2017. We find that 5.1% of heat-related physical illness visits, 5.4% of heat-related mental health visits, and <1% of all-cause ED visits in California were attributable to heat. Communities with lower HPI scores (indicating less healthy conditions) accounted for a higher proportion of ED visits than expected based on their population size, and higher burdens of heat-related morbidity, with four times greater risk of heat-attributable ED visits for physical illness, and two times greater risk for mental health and all-cause visits. This study underscores the disproportionate impact of extreme heat on communities with less healthy conditions and highlights the importance of social determinants of health in shaping heat-related morbidity. Heat-attributable emergency department visits represent a sizable portion of overall morbidity for heat-related outcomes and mental outcomes. Communities with the least healthy conditions have disproportionately higher heat-related morbidity.

entry.title: Breaking the methodological silos: Integrating Mixed-Methods in Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment Lessons learnt from fieldwork in Tenerife

link.title: Breaking the methodological silos: Integrating Mixed-Methods in Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment Lessons learnt from fieldwork in Tenerife
(PDF) Breaking the methodological silos: Integrating Mixed-Methods in Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment Lessons learnt from fieldwork in Tenerife
(XML) Breaking the methodological silos: Integrating Mixed-Methods in Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment Lessons learnt from fieldwork in Tenerife

entry.content:
by Guillermo García Álvarez, Marleen C. de Ruiter

This essay explores the advantages and limitations of using mixed-methods approaches to improve local multi-hazard risk (MHR) assessment and its inherent complexities. By combining desktop analysis, field observations, questionnaires and stakeholder interviews, we demonstrate how each method complements each other to fill data gaps, improve design of methods such as surveys, and increase the understanding of multi-hazard risk dynamics and challenges that become apparent in a local context. Mixed-methods also allow for bridging the gap between scientific modelling and community realities, while reducing reliance on often limited datasets and standardised (often quantitative) methods that are often aimed at larger scale assessments. This combination of quantitative and qualitative methods is illustrated in a recent fieldwork experience, with the objective of suggesting Nature-based Solutions (NBS) to reduce climate risk for the island of Tenerife. In our research agenda, we emphasize the importance of planning ahead when implementing mixed-methods, interdisciplinary collaboration, understanding the feedback loops across methods and incorporating local knowledge to ensure that the adaptation strategies are both evidence-based and socially equitable. This iterative framework aims to enhance the understanding, feasibility and community acceptance of MHR adaptation strategies.

entry.title: Urban heat as a structural development challenge in rapidly growing cities

link.title: Urban heat as a structural development challenge in rapidly growing cities
(PDF) Urban heat as a structural development challenge in rapidly growing cities
(XML) Urban heat as a structural development challenge in rapidly growing cities

entry.content:
by Ansar Khan, Rafiq Hamdi, Tarek Ahmed, Dev Niyogi, Hashem Akbari, Mattheos Santamouris

Urban heat is increasingly emerging as a major constraint on sustainable development, particularly in rapidly growing cities of the Global South. Although urban heat is commonly addressed through local adaptation and urban heat reduction measures such as urban greening, cool and super cool roofs, and building retrofits or passive design, these interventions are increasingly implemented against a backdrop of accelerating planetary warming, fiscal constraints, and persistent socio-economic inequalities. This Essay argues that urban heat should be understood not merely as an environmental, technological, or urban planning challenge, but as a structural development problem arising from the interaction of climate change, rapid urbanization, uneven governance capacity, and political-economic processes that shape vulnerability and adaptive capacity. Drawing on evidence from urban climate, adaptation, development, and climate justice literatures, we examine how escalating heat risks intersect with infrastructure deficits, debt burdens, limited access to climate finance, and unequal access to cooling resources across rapidly growing cities. We show that climate change mitigation and local action, including urban heat reduction and broader adaptation measures, perform distinct but complementary functions, and that local interventions alone cannot overcome the broader climatic and structural conditions that increasingly constrain their effectiveness and scalability. Urban heat risks are further amplified by profound inequalities in exposure, vulnerability, and access to adaptation resources, creating a widening mismatch between those facing the greatest heat burdens and those possessing the greatest capacity to respond. We, therefore, argue that effective urban heat governance requires moving beyond predominantly local and technocratic approaches toward integrated strategies that combine climate change mitigation, equitable climate finance, enhanced fiscal capacity, and multi-level governance. Reframing urban heat as a structural development challenge provides a more comprehensive framework for addressing climate justice, resilience, and long-term urban habitability under a warming climate.

entry.title: Effects of climate change on menstrual health and hygiene: A global mixed-methods systematic review

link.title: Effects of climate change on menstrual health and hygiene: A global mixed-methods systematic review
(PDF) Effects of climate change on menstrual health and hygiene: A global mixed-methods systematic review
(XML) Effects of climate change on menstrual health and hygiene: A global mixed-methods systematic review

entry.content:
by Lauren D’Mello-Guyett, Neelina Jaggarwal, Jane Wilbur, Belen Torondel, Meghna Ranganathan

Menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) encompasses access to menstrual materials; water, sanitation, and disposal facilities; privacy and safety; accurate information; supportive social environments; access to care for menstrual discomfort and disorders; enabling people to manage menstruation with dignity and choice. Climate change is disrupting these interlinked domains, disproportionately affecting women, girls, and people who menstruate. This review synthesises evidence on how climate change affects MHH across diverse climate hazard contexts. We conducted a global mixed-methods systematic review of studies published in English between 1947 and 2025, examining associations between climate-related hazards and MHH. We conducted searches in Medline, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science. Quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies were eligible. Given the heterogeneity in exposures, outcomes, and designs, findings were synthesised narratively. From 3,890 records, 25 studies met inclusion criteria, covering floods (n = 7), air pollution (n = 6), cyclones (n = 3), droughts (n = 3), saltwater intrusion (n = 3), and multiple hazards (n = 4). Flood- and cyclone-related studies reported disrupted access to menstrual materials, damaged water and sanitation infrastructure, reduced privacy and safety, limited access to care for menstrual disorders, and unsupportive social environments characterised by stigma and restricted mobility. Drought and salinity intrusion constrained hygiene practices through reduced water availability and quality, affecting comfort, dignity, and infection risk. Across hazards, studies documented adverse physical outcomes, including dermatological irritation and reproductive or urinary tract infections, alongside psychosocial consequences such as shame, anxiety, and harassment. Air pollution studies linked exposures with earlier menarche and menstrual cycle irregularities. Evidence on extreme heat and several MHH domains, including access to information, was limited. Climate-related hazards undermine multiple, interconnected domains of MHH. The evidence base remains fragmented across hazards, geographies, methods, underscoring the need to integrate MHH into climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, and humanitarian response frameworks and to address critical research gaps related to extreme heat, slow-onset hazards, and equity.

entry.title: The impact of climate change on human health and pharmaceuticals

link.title: The impact of climate change on human health and pharmaceuticals
(PDF) The impact of climate change on human health and pharmaceuticals
(XML) The impact of climate change on human health and pharmaceuticals

entry.content:
by Pono Pono, Alan M. Jones

Climate change and air pollution affect every major organ system, altering both the disease burden and patient responses to pharmaceutical treatments. However, current knowledge on how health systems, patients, healthcare professionals, and governments should prepare for these challenges remains fragmented. This review synthesises evidence on the potential impact of climate change on human health and pharmaceuticals, with the aim of identifying the diseases, populations, and medications most vulnerable, and assessing potential implications for pharmacotherapy. Emerging evidence shows that climate-related stressors, particularly extreme heat, contribute to increased morbidity and mortality and exacerbation of diseases affecting cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, gastrointestinal, renal, and respiratory systems. Furthermore, the review found that high temperature and humidity can affect drug stability, bioavailability, and pharmacokinetics by degrading active pharmaceutical ingredients and altering pharmaceutical formulations, potentially reducing efficacy and increasing the risk of adverse drug events. Older adults, patients with chronic diseases, and those taking medications that impair the thermoregulatory system are particularly at higher risk. In addition, extreme weather events may also disrupt pharmaceutical supply chains, further threatening access to essential medicines. This review finds that climate change has implications for healthcare through increasing disease burden and affecting the effectiveness and safety of medicines. Therefore, there is an urgent need for integrated research to explore the interplay between climate change, therapeutic response, and drug safety to support resilient, climate‑ready healthcare systems.

entry.title: What comes after social tipping? Perspectives from transitions towards net-zero

link.title: What comes after social tipping? Perspectives from transitions towards net-zero
(PDF) What comes after social tipping? Perspectives from transitions towards net-zero
(XML) What comes after social tipping? Perspectives from transitions towards net-zero

entry.content:
by Claudia R. Binder, Alejandro Gomez, Jair Campfens, Maria Anna Hecher, Simón Ladino Cano, Léonard Léchot, Hanbit Lee, Simon Montfort

The world is on track to exceed 1.5 °C of warming. To avoid further temperature increase, accelerated action to decarbonize our societies is needed. Scholars claim that this transition requires surpassing social tipping points (STPs). STPs are defined as non-linear processes of transformative change in social systems, where a small perturbation triggers a response that generates self-amplifying changes in behaviors. While research efforts have focused on analyzing triggers to tipping, we have little understanding of the structures and mechanisms that stabilize a new state after the tipping phase. We argue that post-tipping trajectories rarely converge to a single stable state. Instead, they converge to multiple coexisting (including reversed) states that can exist as spatial patterns and need to be designed-in for stability. Combining insights from ecological systems, where phenomena that occur after tipping have been researched, with empirical evidence on social tipping in transitions towards net zero, we shed light on states after tipping and on how they may be stabilized. Four phenomena shape post-tipping trajectories: (i) lock-in through co-adoption of technologies or feedback loops; (ii) the co-existence of states; (iii) the reversibility of sustainable behaviors; and (iv) infrastructure as a stabilizer of co-existing or new states. We found that a systemic approach that combines technological and social levers to create positive feedback is needed to stabilize a future state. We propose three policy design principles to achieve this: (1) prioritize infrastructure that creates positive lock-ins to new technologies; (2) combine deep (social norms) and shallow (co-adoption of technologies) levers; and (3) target network brokers to bridge adopter and non-adopter groups and establish diffusion structures.

entry.content:
by Fred Tusabe, Sarah Lebu, Musa Manga

Climate change is intensifying rainfall extremes and urban flooding, amplifying public health risks in settings with fragile sanitation and drainage systems. In dense urban informal settlements, floods can overwhelm onsite sanitation and fecal sludge management systems, causing pit inundation, latrine overflow or collapse, and contamination of household environments and water sources. These conditions increase fecal exposure and can amplify cholera risk, particularly where water supply is intermittent and households depend on unsafe sources. Using Lusaka, Zambia as an illustrative case, this essay illustrates flood-driven sanitation failure modes and the feedback loops that can sustain exposure and delay recovery. Lessons from prolonged cholera epidemics in fragile water and sanitation settings underscore that emergency response tools can suppress transmission, but long-term durability depends on sustained investment in safe water and sanitation services and reliable surveillance. Building on recent calls for climate-resilient sanitation, this essay frames sanitation functionality during floods as a core component of epidemic preparedness in LMIC cities, with priorities including flood-resilient containment and fecal sludge services, management of shared sanitation facilities (clear responsibility, cleaning and maintenance systems), routine maintenance and supply-chain reliability, community-engaged early warning and response, and monitoring systems that link service and environmental indicators to health outcomes.

entry.title: Drought vulnerability assessment and its severe impact on crop production and livelihood of people: An empirical modelling of northern Ghana

link.title: Drought vulnerability assessment and its severe impact on crop production and livelihood of people: An empirical modelling of northern Ghana
(PDF) Drought vulnerability assessment and its severe impact on crop production and livelihood of people: An empirical modelling of northern Ghana
(XML) Drought vulnerability assessment and its severe impact on crop production and livelihood of people: An empirical modelling of northern Ghana

entry.content:
by Theophilus Francis Kofitio, Peace Korshiwor Amoatey, Evans Asenso

Climate change is intensifying drought vulnerability in northern Ghana, posing serious risks to crop production, food security, and rural livelihoods in semi-arid regions. This study develops an empirical modelling framework to assess drought vulnerability and impacts at three temporal horizons, 2026–2050, 2051–2075, and 2076–2100, under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. We integrated bias-corrected outputs from five CMIP6 models, MRI-ESM2–0, EC-Earth3, IPSL-CM6A-LR, CESM2, and HadGEM3-GC31-LL, downscaled to 0.25° resolution, with drought indices including the Standardized Precipitation Index SPI, Reconnaissance Drought Index RDI, Normalized Difference Drought Index NDDI, and Soil Moisture Index SMI. These were combined with MODIS-derived Normalized Difference Vegetation Index NDVI, population density, and land use/land cover using GIS-based tools to generate composite drought vulnerability maps. CMIP6 models were validated against reference datasets and showed strong performance for annual precipitation, r = 0.95, RMSE = 3.4 mm, and temperature, r = 0.99, RMSE = 0.47–0.74°C. Results project increasing drought severity, with mean temperature rises of 2.0–3.9°C and rainfall declines up to 19% by 2100. Crop yields for maize, millet, sorghum, and groundnuts are expected to fall by 25–60% by 2050, with maize showing the strongest negative correlation to drought severity, r = –0.72, p < 0.01, confirmed by Mann-Kendall trends at the 95% confidence level. About 84% of the study area is classified as highly vulnerable due to limited adaptive capacity, over 80% dependence on rain-fed agriculture, more than 49% household food insecurity, less than 23% cropland use, and under 5% water body coverage. Significant uncertainties remain in precipitation projections, with some models showing divergent temperature trends, highlighting challenges in modelling climate impacts. The findings underscore the urgent need for district-level drought preparedness, solar-powered irrigation, index insurance, climate-smart agriculture, and Disaster Risk Reduction aligned with UNDRR and Sendai Framework priorities to build resilience in northern Ghana.

entry.title: Fifteen years of regional climate downscaling in CORDEX-Australasia

link.title: Fifteen years of regional climate downscaling in CORDEX-Australasia
(PDF) Fifteen years of regional climate downscaling in CORDEX-Australasia
(XML) Fifteen years of regional climate downscaling in CORDEX-Australasia

entry.content:
by Jason P. Evans, Marcus Thatcher, Daniel Argüeso, Alejandro Di Luca, Ralph Trancoso, Julia Andrys, Sarah Chapman, Giovanni Di Virgilio, Andrew Dowdy, Lluís Fita, Peter B. Gibson, Michael Grose, Emma Howard, Fei Ji, Jatin Kala, Jack Katzfey, Leena Khadke, Omer Mughal, Benjamin Ng, Neelesh Rampal, Christian Stassen, Stephen J. Stuart, Chun Hsu Su, Jozef Syktus, Son C. H. Truong, Harvey Ye

Regional climate modelling plays a central role in understanding and projecting climate change across Australasia, a region characterised by complex topography, diverse climate regimes, and high exposure to climate extremes. Over the past fifteen years, CORDEX-Australasia has coordinated regional climate downscaling under an international framework while operating alongside complementary national and state-based initiatives. Here we synthesise the evolution, achievements, scientific advances, applications, and future priorities of regional climate modelling in the region. Successive CORDEX-CMIP5 and CORDEX-CMIP6 ensembles have produced the largest coordinated high-resolution projection datasets for Australasia. Regional climate models demonstrate clear added value over their driving global climate models, particularly in representing temperature extremes, heavy precipitation, coastal processes, and complex terrain. CMIP6-based projections show robust agreement on substantial 21st-century warming, with uncertainty dominated by emissions scenarios, while precipitation responses remain more regionally heterogeneous. Advances in convection-permitting modelling, benchmarking frameworks, and bias-correction methods have further improved process representation and evaluation. Regional projections now underpin applications in water resources, agriculture, disaster risk reduction, energy, health, and national climate services. Progress has been supported by shared infrastructure through the National Computational Infrastructure and strengthened coordination via the National Partnership for Climate Projections, highlighting strong synergies between State and Federal programs contributing to CORDEX. Key challenges remain including computational demands, persistent model biases, precipitation uncertainty, ensemble design, and translating complex multi-model information into decision-ready guidance. Strategic priorities include kilometre-scale (convection-permitting) modelling, enhanced Earth system coupling, coordinated super-ensembles, responsible integration of artificial intelligence approaches, strengthened observational constraints, and expanded support for vulnerable remote Australian islands and Pacific Island nations. Sustained investment, collaboration, and innovation will be essential to deliver robust, high-resolution climate information for adaptation and resilience across Australasia.

entry.title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based prediction of heatwave trends in northwestern Nigeria

link.title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based prediction of heatwave trends in northwestern Nigeria
(PDF) Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based prediction of heatwave trends in northwestern Nigeria
(XML) Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based prediction of heatwave trends in northwestern Nigeria

entry.content:
by Saadatu Umaru Baba, Abu-hanifa Babati, Zaharaddeen Isa

Climate change has accelerated devastating impacts across the globe, and heatwaves are among the most severe climate extremes threatening human health, agricultural productivity, and ecosystems in northwestern Nigeria. This study aimed to develop a long short-term memory (LSTM) based model to predict heatwave trends in northwestern Nigeria. Historical meteorological data, including daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and relative humidity from 1980 to 2024, were sourced from the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet). Heatwave intensity was measured via heat index (HI) computation, whereas temporal trends were analyzed via the Modified Mann Kendall (MMK) test and Innovative Trend Analysis (ITA). Spatial variation in heatwave intensity was mapped via the Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) method. The LSTM model demonstrated high predictive accuracy during the testing phase, with correlation coefficients (R) ranging from 0.87 to 0.91 and coefficients of determination (R2) ranging from 0.76 to 0.83. The findings revealed a pronounced increase in the frequency and severity of heatwaves across northwestern Nigeria. These findings demonstrate the ability of LSTM based forecasting to provide reliable heatwave predictions and highlight the potential of LSTM models for supporting regional climate adaptation strategies, heat early warning systems, and evidence-based decision making.

entry.title: Too hot to race? Demonstrating heat stress modelling as an adaptation tool for endurance events

link.title: Too hot to race? Demonstrating heat stress modelling as an adaptation tool for endurance events
(PDF) Too hot to race? Demonstrating heat stress modelling as an adaptation tool for endurance events
(XML) Too hot to race? Demonstrating heat stress modelling as an adaptation tool for endurance events

entry.content:
by Kobe Vandelanotte, Bram Du Moulin, Siebe Puynen, Thomas Vergauwen, Sara Top, Steven Caluwaerts

Heat stress is an increasing concern as climate change drives more frequent and intense extreme heat episodes. In particular, participants in outdoor endurance events face a high risk of heat stress related health issues due to prolonged exposure to heat and physical exertion. The Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) is a widely used ISO-standard heat stress index that integrates air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and radiation (both shortwave and longwave) to assess heat stress. Meteorological heat stress metrics such as WBGT can be used to activate heat management plans and to guide or evaluate heat mitigation strategies. To this end, we present a modelling system that combines a numerical weather prediction (NWP) model with a micro-scale radiation model to simulate meter-scale heat stress. We conducted a mobile measurement campaign to collect spatio-temporal WBGT data along the 2024 Dodentocht, a 100-km ultra-endurance hiking event in Belgium. These observations were used to evaluate the modelling system, which demonstrated a reasonable approximation of the observed WBGT along the route and was able to capture some local shade-induced cooling effects. Finally, we used the modelling system as an adaptation tool to simulate various event-management scenarios, including alternative start times, routes, and walking speeds. For the 2024 Dodentocht, starting 3 hours earlier, at 18:00 local time (UTC + 2), would have reduced the cumulative heat-stress exposure, measured as degree hours above 20∘C WBGT, by 35%. The 2023 route exhibited 16.5% more cumulative degree hours above 20∘C WBGT than the 2024 route for the official 21:00 start time under identical meteorological conditions. Our findings demonstrate the potential of high-resolution heat stress modelling systems as reliable and actionable tools to support the development and implementation of effective heat management strategies for outdoor endurance events.

entry.title: Centuries of global heating from Carbon Majors: Dependence on future emissions pathways

link.title: Centuries of global heating from Carbon Majors: Dependence on future emissions pathways
(PDF) Centuries of global heating from Carbon Majors: Dependence on future emissions pathways
(XML) Centuries of global heating from Carbon Majors: Dependence on future emissions pathways

entry.content:
by Dargan M. W. Frierson, Lauren A. Henrie

A range of recent studies have developed methods and data to attribute past and present global temperature change to individual emitters. We perform simulations that attribute the amount of global warming due to corporations, governments and other entities into the future. We utilize the Finite Amplitude Impulse Response (FaIR) model run until 2500, and the Carbon Majors dataset, a database with the emissions history associated with the top 178 oil, gas, coal, and cement producers. We perform counterfactual experiments to calculate the warming attributable to the emissions associated with these entities, using several different future emissions scenarios. The future atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) anomaly attributable to a company’s past emissions is smaller with less ensemble spread in a lower emissions future than it is in a high emissions future. This is due to smaller carbon cycle feedbacks with lower emissions. However, the temperature change from past emissions is larger in a lower emissions future, even with the smaller change in CO2. This is due primarily to the logarithmic sensitivity of CO2 radiative forcing to concentration. Methane concentration post-2080 experiences a negative anomaly, due to a decrease in methane lifetime from elevated temperature, which is a small negative feedback. For any future emissions scenario, the historical emissions from oil, gas, coal, and cement producers affect many aspects of the climate system, including CO2 in the atmosphere and other parts of the carbon cycle, methane, ozone, and stratospheric water vapor. The total radiative forcing induced by these elements stays positive throughout all simulations, which in turn causes positive temperature perturbations. Thus in addition to the damages that have already occurred, we expect the Carbon Majors to be responsible for calculable climate damages for many centuries into the future.

entry.title: A systematic review of biomass and carbon stock estimation approaches: Methods, uncertainties, and emerging opportunities

link.title: A systematic review of biomass and carbon stock estimation approaches: Methods, uncertainties, and emerging opportunities
(PDF) A systematic review of biomass and carbon stock estimation approaches: Methods, uncertainties, and emerging opportunities
(XML) A systematic review of biomass and carbon stock estimation approaches: Methods, uncertainties, and emerging opportunities

entry.content:
by Annissa Muhammed Ahmedin

Accurate quantification of forest biomass and carbon stocks is essential for understanding terrestrial carbon dynamics, climate change mitigation, and improving forest monitoring and greenhouse gas reporting. However, biomass estimation approaches vary considerably in accuracy, scalability, cost, and uncertainty, creating challenges for selecting appropriate methods across ecosystems and spatial scales. This systematic review synthesizes recent advances in forest biomass and carbon stock estimation and evaluates the strengths, limitations, and future directions of major methodological approaches. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses framework, 147 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2025 were reviewed. The studies encompassed field-based measurements, allometric modelling, remote sensing, machine learning, carbon stock models, and integrated multi-source frameworks. The evidence reveals a clear transition from conventional field inventories toward multi-source approaches that integrate ground observations with optical, radar, and Light Detection and Ranging data, advanced modelling, and artificial intelligence. Field measurements and locally calibrated allometric equations remain indispensable for model development and validation, while remote sensing and machine learning enhance spatial coverage and predictive capability. However, estimation accuracy remains strongly influenced by vegetation structure, environmental conditions, data quality, and model transferability. The review demonstrates that no single approach is universally optimal across all ecosystem conditions. Reliable biomass and carbon stock assessments require integrated frameworks that balance accuracy, scalability, cost, and uncertainty through the complementary use of field observations, remote sensing, and advanced modelling techniques. Future research should prioritize expanding biomass reference datasets in underrepresented regions, strengthening model validation and uncertainty quantification, and developing transparent, ecosystem-specific estimation frameworks. Such advances will improve forest carbon accounting, climate mitigation, and evidence-based forest management.

entry.title: Turning points in climate change adaptation: Storytelling and co-producing visions and pathways for creating well-adapted places

link.title: Turning points in climate change adaptation: Storytelling and co-producing visions and pathways for creating well-adapted places
(PDF) Turning points in climate change adaptation: Storytelling and co-producing visions and pathways for creating well-adapted places
(XML) Turning points in climate change adaptation: Storytelling and co-producing visions and pathways for creating well-adapted places

entry.content:
by Emma L. Yule, Joana Avi-Lorie, Pamela Candea, James Porter, Francesca Vantaggiato

Clear adaptation outcomes are essential for driving climate action and assessing progress. However, developing a shared vision of desirable adaptation outcomes and the steps to achieve them requires a shared understanding of what constitutes a well-adapted place and what resources are needed to enable communities to create and implement such visions. The third Scottish National Adaptation Plan (SNAP3) has “communities creating climate resilient places” as a key outcome. Our research draws upon a collaborative workshop that used storytelling techniques to co-produce adaptation visions: developing a shared narrative and identifying ‘turning points’ to put it into practice. Participants included community groups, public sector, and government officials. Key turning points included shifts in governance structures toward local communities inclusion in developing adaptation visions, consistent knowledge-sharing across scales via dedicated platforms/procedures, and enhanced communication and engagement around adaptation narratives at the local level. Unless these measures are implemented, communities will struggle to create the climate-resilient places envisioned in SNAP3. Our findings indicate that local adaptation targets are perceived as potentially useful drivers of adaptation action, but with limitations to their effectiveness: i.e., adaptation targets risk becoming siloed and failing to integrate broader resilience or community priorities. Our research highlights the positive and negative narratives around local adaptation targets, underscoring the need for continuous monitoring and a cautious, place-based approach to their implementation.

entry.title: Adaptation as a catalyst for social change

link.title: Adaptation as a catalyst for social change
(PDF) Adaptation as a catalyst for social change
(XML) Adaptation as a catalyst for social change

entry.content:
by Helen Adams, Giovanna Gini, Richard Dawson, Hayley Fowler, Katie Jenkins, Stephen Jones, Shruthi Krishnamoorthy, Raghav Pant, Shona Paterson, Jaime Toney, Emma Yule, Rosie Witton, Ruth Wolstenholme

Adaptation to climate change is currently characterised by ever-increasing costs to maintain the status quo with respect to climate hazards. This gap is worsened by the fiscal austerity that characterises the current political and economic situation in many countries. These cuts reduce societal resilience through neglected public infrastructure, services and civic spaces generating vulnerability to shocks and an everyday lack of opportunity. Here we argue that without addressing economic austerity, the viability of current approaches to adaptation are severely compromised. Thus, engaging with, and shifting, societal values, norms and objectives in decision-making will be central to a more cost-effective and orderly form of adaptation. This requires amplifying the political voice of communities who often lack the power to effect change. In this framing, adaptation goes beyond (but still includes) responding to hazard, placing greater emphasis on investment in people and advancing their wellbeing. Adaptation becomes a political force driving social change and challenging the logic of economic austerity.

entry.title: Climate action disclosure among companies: Implications for achieving global efforts to limit average global temperature rise to below 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels

link.title: Climate action disclosure among companies: Implications for achieving global efforts to limit average global temperature rise to below 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels

(XML) Climate action disclosure among companies: Implications for achieving global efforts to limit average global temperature rise to below 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels

entry.content:
by Ntule Shimwela, Noah M. Pauline, Catherine A. Masao

Climate action disclosure among companies has gained significant attention in today’s competitive business arena in ensuring business entities effectively and appropriately reduce their greenhouse gas (GHGs) emissions. However, there are inadequate studies that have investigated the extent of corporate climate action disclosure and implications of legal frameworks and corporate attributes in achieving Net Zero Emissions (NZE) targets. To bridge this gap, this study intended to analyse the extent of climate action disclosure among Tanzanian listed companies. Data collection was conducted through document review of 78 sustainability reports, annual reports, and integrated reports published between 2022 and 2024. Further, interviews were conducted with six relevant experts from the listed private corporations and government regulatory authorities. Based on the metrics and targets recommended by the Task on Climate–related Financial Disclosure (TCFD), the climate change disclosure index was developed and used to analyse the extent of climate action disclosure. The distribution of the total mean content score was found to be 18.9%, indicating that the overall extent of climate action disclosure was low. The pattern of distribution was also low across TCFD areas. The low extent of climate action disclosure was attributed to inadequate implementation of relevant frameworks, lack of baseline data and inadequate capacity of companies and experts to perform scenario analysis and define clear climate change Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Therefore, the findings pose important implications for governments, policymakers, and companies to strengthen climate action disclosure.

link.title: Mapping and quantifying engagement levels of governments in IPCC approval meetings by topic from text

(XML) Mapping and quantifying engagement levels of governments in IPCC approval meetings by topic from text

entry.content:
by Patrick Bayer, Lorenzo Crippa, Hannah Hughes, Erlend A. T. Hermansen

We introduce a text-as-data approach from natural language processing that allows mapping and quantifying topic-level variation in engagement levels of member governments in intergovernmental meetings. Building on research that characterizes the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) approval process as a key site for legitimating knowledge input into negotiations under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), we illustrate this method for two key topics from the IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) that became identified policy approaches for national mitigation and adaptation plans in the outcome of the first Global Stocktake of the Paris Agreement: “carbon management” and “nature-based solutions.” Our analysis provides robust evidence that governments’ engagement levels vary by topic, which allows us to nuance existing findings that IPCC meetings are dominated by a few large country delegations across all agenda items. Our proposed method can be applied to other intergovernmental meetings and complements qualitative research methods.

entry.title: Mapping justice claims for solar geoengineering

link.title: Mapping justice claims for solar geoengineering
(PDF) Mapping justice claims for solar geoengineering
(XML) Mapping justice claims for solar geoengineering

entry.content:
by Sikina Jinnah, Portia Adade Williams, Catriona McKinnon

Solar geoengineering is a set of controversial emerging technologies that seek to cool the planet by reflecting sunlight. These technologies may be able to reduce the worst impacts of climate change by lowering global temperatures temporarily. They also come with great risks, including as related to technological lock in and mitigation deterrence, among others. Balancing these potential risks and benefits demands a careful interrogation of justice and ethics. Unlike many scholars who assert a clear justice landscape, we argue here that the terrain is complicated, nuanced, and not fully mapped. In this essay we explore three core narratives at the intersection of solar geoengineering and justice: intergenerational ethics; participatory justice; and recognitional/reparational justice. We conclude that discussions, debates, and research surrounding justice in the solar geoengineering space should be more focused on the justice of the procedures and practices used in this space, rather than on the justice of specific outcomes that could be secured by solar geoengineering. In focusing on just processes and practices for technological innovation and governance we could enhance our capacity to co-create a world where any decisions on solar geoengineering, whether to ban it or move it forward, are based on thoughtful, ethical, and participatory decision-making that speaks to the interests of all people potentially affected by solar geoengineering.
